profile.title: Meal-Timing and Adherence Barriers in a 43-Year-Old Man with Hyperlipidemia and Prediabetes
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment for a stoic, under-reporting patient with hyperlipidemia and prediabetes whose real problem - skipping meals all day then eating one large late-night meal - is intertwined with social isolation since his divorce. A built-in patient-versus-record mismatch (his self-reported 'I take my inhalers fine' versus a pharmacy refill record showing 7-10+ day gaps in his controller inhaler, undisclosed to his pulmonologist) gives learners practice spotting and gently exploring discrepancies without derailing the nutrition-focused visit. The case emphasizes motivational-interviewing skills to negotiate a single small, concrete change consistent with the patient's preparation stage of change, rather than overwhelming him with a full diet overhaul.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Crestwood Village, New Jersey, seated at his kitchen table

patient.name: Gordon Bergnaum
patient.occupation: Former warehouse inventory clerk, now not in the labor force due to disability-related early retirement
patient.appearance: A stocky, soft-spoken man sitting at a cluttered kitchen table, wearing a faded flannel shirt. He has dry, flaky patches visible on his forearms, keeps his arms crossed or hands folded, and gives brief, even-keeled answers without much facial animation. A cat occasionally wanders into frame.

persona.personality: Stoic, even-keeled, and self-sufficient; tends to minimize symptoms and problems, rarely volunteers opinions or complaints unless gently drawn out
persona.communicationStyle: Soft-spoken with brief, practical answers; frequently defers with phrases like 'whatever you think is best'; opens up slightly only when talking about his grandkids or his garden
persona.emotionalState: Calm and resigned on the surface, mildly guarded about anything that feels like criticism of his habits, quietly lonely underneath the stoicism
persona.background: Gordon is a 43-year-old divorced man living in Crestwood Village, New Jersey, in a household that technically includes five people through a shared family arrangement, though he spends much of his week alone. He used to work as a warehouse inventory clerk until a disability led him to leave the workforce early. He grew up in a working-class New Jersey family where meals were simple and practical - meatloaf, canned vegetables, whatever was on sale - and he's carried that practical, no-fuss attitude about food into adulthood. He keeps a small vegetable garden in the summer that he's proud of, though he admits he rarely gets around to eating much of what he grows. He has a cat he feeds on a strict schedule - more consistently, he jokes, than he feeds himself. He values his independence and doesn't like making a fuss about his health, having 'just gotten on with it' through various chronic issues since childhood.
speechExamples: Whatever you think is best, doc.
I'm fine, really - don't make a big deal out of it.
I just never got hungry during the day, so I eat when I finally sit down at night.
It's not lonely, that's just how it is now.
I guess I only reach for the inhaler when my chest feels tight - didn't think that was wrong.
concerns: His cholesterol numbers creeping up at his last visit
Being lectured by his adult children about his habits
Not wanting to seem like he's falling apart or becoming a burden

scenario.studentBrief: You are joining a telehealth video visit as the dietetics student. The patient is Gordon Bergnaum, a 43-year-old man following up for nutrition counseling related to his hyperlipidemia and prediabetes. Review his chart before the call. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment, understand his eating pattern and barriers, and work with him toward one concrete next step he feels ready to take.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Nutrition follow-up visit for hyperlipidemia and prediabetes management
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah - I'm here. I guess I'm just following up about my cholesterol and whatever else. I eat one big meal at night and don't really do breakfast, if that's what you're asking.
tasks: Take a focused diet history, including meal timing, portion sizes, beverage intake, and typical food choices
Review available anthropometric data, labs, and medication/record information relevant to his nutrition status
Explore the psychosocial and practical barriers behind his current eating pattern using a patient-centred, nonjudgmental approach
Identify any mismatches between what the patient reports and what the record shows, and address them sensitively
Negotiate and document one specific, patient-chosen first step consistent with his readiness to change, using ADIME format

actions.name: 24-hour dietary recall / meal pattern assessment
actions.result: Patient reports no breakfast or lunch most days. First intake is coffee starting mid-morning. Around 6pm, sometimes a snack of chips or crackers. Main meal after 9pm: typically a frozen lasagna or meatloaf dinner, or deli ham and cheese on white bread, with potato chips; reports occasionally having seconds. Minimal water intake during the day, some water with the evening meal.

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage-of-change assessment
actions.result: Patient identifies himself as ready to make a change and wants one specific, manageable step to start this week rather than a full overhaul of his diet. Consistent with the preparation stage of change.

actions.name: Social/household context screen
actions.result: Patient reports living in a household of five on a shared basis but spends much of his week at the residence alone, particularly at mealtimes. Describes seeing people 3-5 times per week overall.

actions.name: Physical activity assessment
actions.result: Patient reports no structured exercise since a knee problem a few years ago. Describes activity as walking to the mailbox and light household chores.

actions.name: Alcohol and tobacco use screen
actions.result: Patient reports quitting smoking about 8 years ago. Reports drinking one to two beers on weekend days, none during the week.

actions.name: Medication-taking routine review (timing relative to meals)
actions.result: Patient reports taking lisinopril with whatever he first eats or drinks in the day. Reports taking ferrous sulfate daily but says some nights he takes it late with his big meal instead of in the morning; mentions his stomach bothers him some nights after taking it.

actions.name: Inhaler use pattern review
actions.result: Patient reports he 'takes his inhalers fine' and uses the daily controller inhaler 'when he feels like he needs it,' saying this is rare. States he hasn't had any flare-ups worth mentioning.

actions.name: Sodium intake source screen (processed/convenience foods)
actions.result: Patient identifies deli ham and cheese, potato chips, and frozen prepared dinners as near-daily components of his evening meal. Does not add table salt beyond what's in packaged foods.

actions.name: Hydration pattern assessment
actions.result: Patient reports several cups of black coffee starting mid-morning, with water mainly limited to what he drinks alongside his evening meal. Says he 'doesn't think about drinking water much' otherwise.

artifacts.title: Endocrinology Follow-up Note (Prior Visit)
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Hennessey, Endocrinology
artifacts.body: 43 y/o male seen for prediabetes and hyperlipidemia follow-up. Patient reports feeling well overall, denies polyuria/polydipsia. Discussed lifestyle modification including meal regularity and reduced processed food intake; patient agreeable but noncommittal about specifics. Continue simvastatin 10mg daily, lisinopril 10mg daily. Referred to nutrition for dietary counseling given overweight BMI and borderline A1c. Will recheck labs in 6 weeks. Asthma and dermatitis stable per patient report; no acute complaints voiced at this visit.

artifacts.title: Pharmacy Refill History - Fluticasone Propionate MDI (Flovent) 0.044 mg/actuation
artifacts.author: Crestwood Pharmacy
artifacts.body: Refill pattern over past 6 months shows the controller inhaler consistently being refilled later than the expected 30-day supply interval, with gaps of 7 to 12 days between when one canister should have run out (based on twice-daily dosing) and the next refill pickup. One notable gap of 10 days occurred in January 2026, overlapping with a documented sinusitis flare. No refill gaps are noted for the albuterol rescue inhaler, which has been refilled at intervals consistent with occasional as-needed use.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused diet/meal-pattern history that reveals skipped breakfast and lunch followed by a single large late-night meal, and link this pattern to convenience-food and sodium intake.
Review relevant anthropometric data and laboratory results (weight/BMI, HbA1c, lipid panel, renal panel, CBC) and relate findings to the patient's eating pattern and chronic disease management.

Use a nonjudgmental, patient-centred approach to uncover medication-taking routines, including inhaler use and iron supplement timing, and identify discrepancies between self-report and the medical record.
Explore psychosocial and practical barriers underlying the late-meal pattern, including social isolation after divorce and family dynamics, using a respectful and nonjudgmental approach.
Assess the patient's stage of readiness to change and negotiate one specific, patient-chosen first step consistent with his stated preference for a single manageable goal.
Screen for additional lifestyle factors (physical activity, alcohol/tobacco use, hydration) relevant to a comprehensive nutrition assessment.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Altered nutrition-related behavior: disordered meal timing (skipped breakfast/lunch with a single large late-night meal) in a man with hyperlipidemia and prediabetes, compounded by undisclosed controller-inhaler nonadherence and underlying loneliness since his divorce.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Undesirable food choices (excessive sodium/convenience foods) related to limited meal planning and living alone, as evidenced by diet history of deli meats, chips, and frozen entrees.

Nutrition diagnosis: Irregular meal pattern (skipped breakfast and lunch, one large meal after 9pm) related to loss of routine after divorce and lack of daytime appetite cues, as evidenced by patient report of 'one big meal' eaten late.
Nutrition diagnosis: Inadequate fluid intake related to habitual reliance on coffee, as evidenced by patient report of minimal water intake.

Behavioral/psychosocial contributor (not a nutrition diagnosis but relevant context): medication nonadherence (fluticasone controller inhaler used symptomatically rather than scheduled) that the patient has not disclosed to his pulmonologist.
Consider but not primary: inadequate energy intake overall - unlikely given overweight BMI and large caloric load concentrated at night.
keyFindings: BMI 27.7 kg/m2 (overweight), weight 87.6 kg, height 177.9 cm
Fasting glucose 93 mg/dL (normal) but HbA1c 5.9% (prediabetic range, >=5.7)
Total cholesterol 207.7 mg/dL and LDL 126 mg/dL both above goal; HDL 52.7 and triglycerides 143.4 within normal limits
BP 117/96 mmHg - diastolic elevated despite normal systolic
eGFR 67 mL/min/1.73m2 - mildly reduced, worth noting for sodium/protein counseling but not a current nutrition diagnosis driver
Diet history: skips breakfast and lunch, single large meal after 9 pm consisting of frozen entrees, deli meats, chips, with occasional seconds
Hydration pattern: several cups of black coffee daily, minimal water

Reports taking the fluticasone inhaler 'when I feel like I need it' rather than twice daily; pharmacy refill record shows gaps of 7-10+ days without refill pickup, including during a documented sinusitis flare, which the patient has not disclosed to his pulmonologist
Patient reports eating alone most nights since his divorce and describes the late meal as 'the one quiet comfort' of his day
Stage of change: preparation - patient explicitly wants one small, concrete first step rather than a full overhaul
plan: Complete a full ADIME-format nutrition assessment including 24-hour recall and typical day pattern, confirming meal timing, portions, and beverage intake
Review available anthropometric and lab data (weight/BMI, HbA1c, lipid panel, BP, eGFR) in the context of the diet history to formulate the nutrition diagnosis (PES statement)
Gently explore the psychosocial context of the late meal (loneliness, living alone part of the week, family dynamics) without pushing the patient past his comfort level

Review the pharmacy/medication record for the fluticasone inhaler and compare it with the patient's self-report to identify the adherence mismatch; flag for communication with his pulmonologist rather than attempting to manage the inhaler directly

Negotiate one specific, patient-chosen behavioral goal consistent with his stage of change (e.g., adding a small daytime snack, moving dinner earlier by 1-2 hours, swapping chips for a lower-sodium side) and set a realistic follow-up timeframe

Document using ADIME format: Assessment (diet history, anthropometrics, labs, psychosocial factors), Diagnosis (PES statement), Intervention (agreed single goal, education given), Monitoring/Evaluation (plan to reassess at next visit)
redFlags: Diastolic BP 96 mmHg is elevated and should be flagged for the medical team though not primarily a nutrition action item
HbA1c in prediabetic range trending upward risk given current eating pattern
eGFR 67 (mildly reduced) warrants noting for future sodium/protein guidance and medical follow-up

Undisclosed controller-inhaler nonadherence during a symptomatic sinusitis period is a patient-safety concern that should be communicated back to the referring/primary clinical team with the patient's awareness
Social isolation at mealtimes may be an ongoing emotional vulnerability, not simply a dietary habit
educationPoints: Explain in plain language how skipping meals all day and eating one very large meal late at night can affect blood sugar, cholesterol, and sleep, without shaming the pattern
Discuss how deli meats, chips, and frozen entrees contribute to sodium intake relevant to his blood pressure, offering simple swaps rather than a full overhaul
Normalize that one small, concrete change (not a complete diet rebuild) is an appropriate and effective starting point given his stated readiness
Encourage him to mention his actual inhaler-use pattern to his pulmonologist, framing it as useful information for his asthma care rather than a confession of failure

Validate the role of eating alone in shaping his current pattern, and explore (without insisting) whether any small routine shift (e.g., eating with family when available) might support a healthier timing without taking away his sense of autonomy

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes his inhalers fine and only uses the daily fluticasone (Flovent) controller inhaler 'when he feels like he needs it,' describing this as rare, with no gaps reported to his pulmonologist.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history for fluticasone propionate MDI shows refill gaps consistent with stretches of 7-10+ days without the medication, including during a documented sinusitis flare.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely underreport nonadherence to maintenance medications, especially when they believe symptom-based use is reasonable; cross-checking refill records against self-report is essential before counseling, and discrepancies should be raised gently and relayed to the prescribing clinician rather than confronted.
